label: Idea
name: fascism
summary:
Fascism is a far-right, authoritarian, and ultranationalist political ideology and movement that rose to prominence in early-20th-century Europe. Characterized by dictatorial power, suppression of opposition, subordination of individual interests to the state, and intense nationalism, fascism emerged from the dislocations of World War I and represented a revolutionary rejection of both liberal democracy and Marxist internationalism.

The term derives from the Italian fascio (bundle/fasces), the ancient Roman symbol of authority adopted by Benito Mussolini when he founded the Fasci Italiani di Combattimento in 1919. Mussolini's March on Rome (1922) brought the first fascist government to power. Adolf Hitler's National Socialism — drawing from Italian fascism while adding racial antisemitism as its core ideology — produced the Nazi regime (1933–1945), the Holocaust, and World War II. Fascist or proto-fascist movements flourished across Europe (Spain, Portugal, Romania, Hungary) and Latin America in the 1930s and 1940s.

Fascism's intellectual genealogy is disputed — it drew from Social Darwinism, Sorel's cult of violence, syndicalism, and romantic nationalism — but its structural features are consistent: the leadership principle (Führerprinzip), national community (Volksgemeinschaft) overriding individual rights, the glorification of war, and the elimination of political opposition. The defeat of the Axis powers in 1945 discredited fascism as a governing ideology, but neofascist movements have periodically revived in various forms. Scholars debate whether 'fascism' can be applied beyond its interwar European context.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Fascism had a significant regional impact in Europe during the interwar period, contributing to the outbreak of World War II and shaping the course of European history. Its authoritarian ideology and nationalist policies led to the rise of dictatorial regimes across the continent.

causes: World War I's trauma — mass death, national humiliation, and social dislocation creating the radicalized mass politics fascism exploited
Fear of Bolshevik revolution driving conservative elites to support fascist movements as a bulwark against Marxist power
Weimar Germany's economic crisis (hyperinflation 1923, Great Depression 1929–33) destroying the legitimacy of liberal democracy
Social Darwinism and romantic nationalism providing the ideological raw material that fascist theorists synthesized
effects: Mussolini's Italy (1922–1945) — first fascist state; template for subsequent movements
Nazi Germany (1933–1945) and the Holocaust — industrialized genocide of 6 million Jews and 5 million others
World War II (1939–1945) — fascist expansionism triggering the deadliest conflict in human history
Post-war international order — the UN, the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, and NATO all designed as responses to fascism's crimes
